blocks.text: ShellBench 是我们与 The OpenClaw Foundation、Parsewave、Hugging Face、Red Hat 和 UC Berkeley 的研究人员合作开发的新基准测试。它基于超过 1000 万条匿名的真实 AI 智能体交互记录，衡量 AI 智能体在人们实际委托给它们的日常工作中的表现。

inlines.text: ShellBench 是我们与 The OpenClaw Foundation、Parsewave、Hugging Face、Red Hat 和 UC Berkeley 的研究人员合作开发的新基准测试。它基于超过 1000 万条匿名的真实 AI 智能体交互记录，衡量 AI 智能体在人们实际委托给它们的日常工作中的表现。

blocks.text: ShellBench 评估了十二个模型：GPT-6 Astra、Claude Fable 5.2、GPT-6.1 Sol、Gemini 4 Carbon、Muse Wonder Full、Claude Opus 5.5、Muse Wonder 1.0、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash、Claude Sonnet 5.5、Kimi K3.1 Pro、DeepSeek V4 Pro 和 GPT-6 Luna。这些模型在五种智能体运行框架下接受测试：Claude Code、Codex、Hermes、OpenClaw 和 Pi。

blocks.text: 在日常工作上测试智能体

inlines.text: 在日常工作上测试智能体

blocks.text: 大多数 AI 基准测试都围绕定义明确的问题设计，比如回答一个问题、解一道数学题，或者写出能通过测试的代码。但真实用户为日常工作提出的真实请求，很少这么有条理。更常见的情况是，你让智能体去找一份文档的最新版本、核对来自几十个来源的开支，或者根据一长串邮件往来准备一封回复。

blocks.text: ShellBench 测试的正是这类工作。

inlines.text: ShellBench 测试的正是这类工作。

blocks.text: 每个测试场景都从一个简短的请求开始（在 90 项按评分标准打分的任务中，请求中位数只有 43 个词），并配有一个贴近现实的工作区（这些任务的工作区中位数是 188 个文件），其中包括邮件、日历导出文件、电子表格、聊天记录、收据、保存的网页和 PDF。

blocks.text: 大多数任务都会设置一个复杂因素，比如过时的记录、看起来相似的账户、相互矛盾的信息，甚至可能是恶意的指令。

blocks.text: 在 77 项任务中，有 87 条标准用来检查答案是否点明了自己用到的文件，包括那些用于裁定信息冲突的记录。晚餐规划任务就说明了这一点为什么重要。

inlines.text: 在 77 项任务中，有 87 条标准用来检查答案是否点明了自己用到的文件，包括那些用于裁定信息冲突的记录。晚餐规划任务就说明了这一点为什么重要。

blocks.text: 例如，在一项晚餐规划任务中，531 次尝试里有 522 次选对了餐厅，但有 331 次失败，唯一原因就是推荐结果没有点明支撑该团体预算或时间安排的文件。只有 152 次满足了全部要求。

inlines.text: 例如，在一项晚餐规划任务中，531 次尝试里有 522 次选对了餐厅，但有 331 次失败，唯一原因就是推荐结果没有点明支撑该团体预算或时间安排的文件。只有 152 次满足了全部要求。

blocks.text: 检索信息、对信息进行推理，以及把信息一直保留到最终答案，是三种不同的能力。智能体可以检索到正确的信息，却仍然没能在最终答案中把它保留下来。

inlines.text: 检索信息、对信息进行推理，以及把信息一直保留到最终答案，是三种不同的能力。智能体可以检索到正确的信息，却仍然没能在最终答案中把它保留下来。

blocks.text: 对开发者来说，这意味着提升下一代智能体不能只靠减少幻觉，还要改进智能体追踪需求、保留重要上下文、核验完整性以及说明所用证据的方式。

inlines.text: 4. 安全失误可能藏在看似普通的任务里

blocks.text: ShellBench 还专门关注安全。它的任务纳入了正常工作流程中可能出现的风险，包括钓鱼尝试、欺诈性付款指令、敏感信息和不可逆操作。

blocks.text: ShellBench 发现，执行框架会改变智能体的工作方式，包括它们处理多少 token、多久修改一次输出，以及完成任务需要多长时间。结果显示，即使任务完成率接近，执行时间也存在显著差异。

blocks.text: 对于运行智能体的人来说，关键结论是：最佳配置取决于模型选择、执行时间、可用工具，以及智能体如何把你的工作当作一个整体来处理。

Ask an AI agent to summarize a document, and it will probably do a decent job. Ask it to reconcile a handful of receipts against a spreadsheet, check which information is current, flag a suspicious payment request, and explain how it reached its answer? Maybe not so well.

inlines.text: Ask an AI agent to summarize a document, and it will probably do a decent job. Ask it to reconcile a handful of receipts against a spreadsheet, check which information is current, flag a suspicious payment request, and explain how it reached its answer? Maybe not so well.

blocks.text: This kind of realistic test, one that expects an agent not just to find the right information but also to keep track of it along the way, is exactly what we’re launching ShellBench to evaluate.

inlines.text: This kind of realistic test, one that expects an agent not just to find the right information but also to keep track of it along the way, is exactly what we’re launching ShellBench to evaluate.

blocks.text: Shellbench is a new benchmark developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley. It draws on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to measure how AI agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them.

inlines.text: Shellbench is a new benchmark developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley. It draws on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to measure how AI agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them.

blocks.text: ShellBench evaluated twelve models: GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon, Muse Wonder Full, Claude Opus 5.5, Muse Wonder 1.0, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Kimi K3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Pro, and GPT-6 Luna. These were tested across five agent harnesses: Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, and Pi.

blocks.text: Testing agents on everyday work

inlines.text: Testing agents on everyday work

blocks.text: Most AI benchmarks are designed around clearly defined problems, like answering a question, solving a math problem, or writing test-passing code. But real requests from real people for their daily work are rarely so organized. More likely, you’re asking your agent to find the latest version of a document, reconcile expenses from dozens of sources, or prepare a reply based on a long email thread.

inlines.text: Most AI benchmarks are designed around clearly defined problems, like answering a question, solving a math problem, or writing test-passing code. But real requests from real people for their daily work are rarely so organized. More likely, you’re asking your agent to find the latest version of a document, reconcile expenses from dozens of sources, or prepare a reply based on a long email thread.

blocks.text: ShellBench tests this kind of work.

inlines.text: ShellBench tests this kind of work.

blocks.text: Each tested scenario starts with a short request (median of just 43 words across the 90 rubric-graded tasks) and a realistic workspace (median of 188 files across those tasks), including emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, chat logs, receipts, saved web pages, and PDFs.

inlines.text: Each tested scenario starts with a short request (median of just 43 words across the 90 rubric-graded tasks) and a realistic workspace (median of 188 files across those tasks), including emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, chat logs, receipts, saved web pages, and PDFs.

blocks.text: Most tasks introduce a complication, like outdated records, similar-looking accounts, conflicting information, and even potentially malicious instructions.

inlines.text: Most tasks introduce a complication, like outdated records, similar-looking accounts, conflicting information, and even potentially malicious instructions.

blocks.text: The agent has to find the right evidence, complete the request, avoid phishing traps, and produce a verifiable answer.

inlines.text: The agent has to find the right evidence, complete the request, avoid phishing traps, and produce a verifiable answer.

blocks.text: Of those 100 tasks, 90 are rubric-graded against 721 criteria (including 381 safety criteria), and 10 are code-tested. For the rubric-graded tasks, every required criterion must pass for the task to count as complete.

blocks.text: 1. Even the strongest agents have a long way to go

inlines.text: 1. Even the strongest agents have a long way to go

blocks.text: Averaged across harnesses, even the highest-performing models successfully completed only about six in ten tasks.

inlines.text: Averaged across harnesses, even the highest-performing models successfully completed only about six in ten tasks.

blocks.text: GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%, followed by Claude Fable 5.2 at 61.9% and GPT-6.1 Sol at 61.4%. Just 1.1 percentage points separated the top three.

inlines.text: GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%, followed by Claude Fable 5.2 at 61.9% and GPT-6.1 Sol at 61.4%. Just 1.1 percentage points separated the top three.

blocks.text: That means even the leading models failed to satisfy every requirement on roughly four in ten attempts.

inlines.text: That means even the leading models failed to satisfy every requirement on roughly four in ten attempts.

blocks.text: In practice, this means if an agent is reconciling payments, identifying the latest instructions, or preparing a complete report, one missing requirement can change whether the work is ready to use.

blocks.text: 2. Getting the facts right isn’t enough if you leave out the evidence

inlines.text: 2. Getting the facts right isn’t enough if you leave out the evidence

blocks.text: One of ShellBench’s most striking findings concerns what agents do after locating relevant information.

inlines.text: One of ShellBench’s most striking findings concerns what agents do after locating relevant information.

blocks.text: Across 77 tasks, 87 criteria check whether the answer names the files it used, including the records that settle conflicting information. The dinner-planning task shows why this matters.

inlines.text: Across 77 tasks, 87 criteria check whether the answer names the files it used, including the records that settle conflicting information. The dinner-planning task shows why this matters.

blocks.text: For example, in one dinner-planning task, 522 of 531 attempts picked the right restaurant, but 331 failed solely because the recommendation didn’t name the files supporting the group’s budget or timing. Only 152 met every requirement.

blocks.text: Retrieving information, reasoning about it, and preserving it through to the final answer are different capabilities. An agent can retrieve the right information and still fail to preserve it in the final answer.

blocks.text: For developers, this suggests that improving the next generation of agents won’t be limited to reducing hallucinations. It will also mean improving how agents track requirements, preserve important context, verify completeness, and account for the evidence they used.

blocks.text: 3. Getting it right once doesn’t mean getting it right consistently

inlines.text: 3. Getting it right once doesn’t mean getting it right consistently

blocks.text: ShellBench also tested reliability across repeated attempts.

inlines.text: ShellBench also tested reliability across repeated attempts.

blocks.text: Averaged across five harnesses in the 100-task evaluation, GPT-6 Astra successfully completed 75.1% of tasks at least once across three attempts.

inlines.text: Averaged across five harnesses in the 100-task evaluation, GPT-6 Astra successfully completed 75.1% of tasks at least once across three attempts.

blocks.text: But it completed only 48.8% successfully on all three attempts. Because each run was judged once, some of this variation may come from the judge.

inlines.text: But it completed only 48.8% successfully on all three attempts. Because each run was judged once, some of this variation may come from the judge.

blocks.text: Notably, this shows that, while an agent might be capable of accomplishing a task, that doesn’t necessarily mean it will continue accomplishing it reliably. Only repeated evaluations can reveal if it does.

inlines.text: Notably, this shows that, while an agent might be capable of accomplishing a task, that doesn’t necessarily mean it will continue accomplishing it reliably. Only repeated evaluations can reveal if it does.

blocks.text: An agent that succeeds once but fails every third time on the same assignment still requires oversight.

blocks.text: 4. Safety failures can hide inside otherwise ordinary tasks

inlines.text: 4. Safety failures can hide inside otherwise ordinary tasks

blocks.text: ShellBench also specifically focuses on safety. Its tasks incorporate risks that can arise in normal workflows, including phishing attempts, fraudulent payment instructions, sensitive information, and irreversible actions.

inlines.text: ShellBench also specifically focuses on safety. Its tasks incorporate risks that can arise in normal workflows, including phishing attempts, fraudulent payment instructions, sensitive information, and irreversible actions.

blocks.text: The 100-task evaluation includes 381 individual safety criteria.

inlines.text: The 100-task evaluation includes 381 individual safety criteria.

blocks.text: Across all 53,100 runs, 15.7% failed at least one safety check. Harness choice made little overall difference to safety. Even among the 26,151 runs that met every correctness criterion, 2,589 (9.9%) still failed a safety requirement.

inlines.text: Across all 53,100 runs, 15.7% failed at least one safety check. Harness choice made little overall difference to safety. Even among the 26,151 runs that met every correctness criterion, 2,589 (9.9%) still failed a safety requirement.

blocks.text: An agent’s overall task-completion rate doesn’t eliminate the need to examine safety across a complete workflow, reflecting the ongoing work necessary for the entire agent ecosystem.

blocks.text: 5. The model matters more than the harness, but the harness still matters

inlines.text: 5. The model matters more than the harness, but the harness still matters

blocks.text: Across the models tested in all five harnesses, the median gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring models within a harness was 45.7 percentage points.

inlines.text: Across the models tested in all five harnesses, the median gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring models within a harness was 45.7 percentage points.

blocks.text: Switching harnesses while keeping the model fixed produced a smaller median gap of 6.2 points. Among the five highest-scoring models, the gaps narrowed to 15.2 points for model choice and 9.9 for harness choice.

inlines.text: Switching harnesses while keeping the model fixed produced a smaller median gap of 6.2 points. Among the five highest-scoring models, the gaps narrowed to 15.2 points for model choice and 9.9 for harness choice.

blocks.text: The results suggest that the underlying model is a stronger predictor of task completion than the harness surrounding it, at least for the models and tasks tested.

inlines.text: The results suggest that the underlying model is a stronger predictor of task completion than the harness surrounding it, at least for the models and tasks tested.

blocks.text: But that doesn’t make the harness interchangeable.

inlines.text: But that doesn’t make the harness interchangeable.

blocks.text: ShellBench found that harnesses changed how agents worked, including how many tokens they processed, how often they revised their outputs, and how long they took to complete tasks. The results show substantial differences in execution time even where task-completion rates are close.

inlines.text: ShellBench found that harnesses changed how agents worked, including how many tokens they processed, how often they revised their outputs, and how long they took to complete tasks. The results show substantial differences in execution time even where task-completion rates are close.

blocks.text: For people running agents, the takeaway is that the best configuration depends on model choice, execution time, available tools, and the way an agent handles your work as a collective whole.

blocks.text: 6. Open-source harnesses hold their own

inlines.text: 6. Open-source harnesses hold their own

blocks.text: If the underlying model matters more than the harness, that raises another question: does using an open-source harness mean trading away performance? ShellBench confirmed it did not.

blocks.text: That’s a spread of 2.36 percentage points between the highest- and lowest-scoring harness averages, showing that open-source harnesses can deliver competitive task completion with a proprietary alternative when tested on the same models.

blocks.text: 7. Capability and cost don’t always move together

inlines.text: 7. Capability and cost don’t always move together

blocks.text: The three highest-performing models were separated by just 1.1 percentage points in average pass rate, but the estimated cost per run varied considerably. GPT-6 Astra passed 62.5% of tasks at $1.10 per run, Claude Fable 5.2 passed 61.9% at $0.83, and GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% at $0.19.

inlines.text: The three highest-performing models were separated by just 1.1 percentage points in average pass rate, but the estimated cost per run varied considerably. GPT-6 Astra passed 62.5% of tasks at $1.10 per run, Claude Fable 5.2 passed 61.9% at $0.83, and GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% at $0.19.

blocks.text: That puts GPT-6.1 Sol within 1.1 points of the highest pass rate at roughly one-sixth the estimated per-run cost. At the lower end, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash passed 39.7% of tasks at about five cents per run. (Estimates use recorded token usage and study token prices and exclude grading costs.)

blocks.text: What this means for the industry

inlines.text: What this means for the industry

blocks.text: We didn’t build OpenClaw around the idea that one model or one agent configuration would always be the best.

inlines.text: We didn’t build OpenClaw around the idea that one model or one agent configuration would always be the best.

blocks.text: Different models have different strengths and new ones arrive constantly. People should be able to choose what runs their agent, where it runs, and which tools it can use.

inlines.text: Different models have different strengths and new ones arrive constantly. People should be able to choose what runs their agent, where it runs, and which tools it can use.

blocks.text: ShellBench is designed for this reality.

inlines.text: ShellBench is designed for this reality.

blocks.text: Moreover, openness and capability aren’t mutually exclusive. People should be able to choose an open, extensible system without assuming they’ll have to settle for substantially weaker results. And performance alone doesn’t settle which harness someone should use.

inlines.text: Moreover, openness and capability aren’t mutually exclusive. People should be able to choose an open, extensible system without assuming they’ll have to settle for substantially weaker results. And performance alone doesn’t settle which harness someone should use.

blocks.text: The results also expose work that still needs to be done, particularly around completeness, reliability, safety, and execution time. As we build the agentic future in the open, we want to measure those gaps openly, and help the rest of the industry do the same.
